rows.source: HSE beauty and nail-bar COSHH controls
rows.verified: Some ingredients in beauty and cleaning products can irritate skin and lead to dermatitis.

rows.source: HSE beauty and nail-bar COSHH controls
rows.verified: Liquids and powders used in acrylic nail systems can cause skin allergy and occupational asthma.

rows.source: HSE beauty and nail-bar COSHH controls
rows.verified: Dust generated when filing artificial nails can cause wheezing, chest tightness and asthma.

rows.source: HSE beauty and nail-bar COSHH controls
rows.verified: Acrylic fumes can cause headache, dizziness and nausea.

rows.source: HSE beauty and nail-bar COSHH controls
rows.verified: Blood and tissue residues from piercing or tattooing can create an infection hazard.

rows.source: HSE beauty and nail-bar COSHH controls
rows.verified: Beauty workplaces should maintain good general ventilation and use work techniques that minimise contact, leaks and spills.

rows.source: HSE beauty and nail-bar COSHH controls
rows.verified: HSE nail-bar guidance describes extraction, including extractor hoods or downdraught tables, to control dust and odour exposure.

rows.source: HSE beauty and nail-bar COSHH controls
rows.verified: Good hand care and task-appropriate gloves, aprons or eye protection may be required alongside engineering controls.

rows.source: HSE beauty and nail-bar COSHH controls
rows.verified: Beauty-treatment risk depends on product chemistry, treatment type, ventilation, extraction, contact duration, hygiene and worker sensitisation.

rows.source: HSE beauty and nail-bar COSHH controls
rows.verified: Beauty and nail-bar evidence is product-, task-, exposure-, workplace- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.

rows.source: HSE dry-cleaning solvent controls
rows.verified: HSE provides a dedicated COSHH control sheet for dry cleaning with chlorinated solvent.

rows.source: HSE dry-cleaning solvent controls
rows.verified: Dry-cleaning spot treatment is covered by a separate HSE COSHH control sheet because its tasks and exposure routes differ from machine cleaning.

rows.source: HSE dry-cleaning solvent controls
rows.verified: Tetrachloroethene is also known as tetrachloroethylene or perchloroethylene and is used as a dry-cleaning solvent.

rows.source: HSE dry-cleaning solvent controls
rows.verified: HSE records a Great Britain workplace exposure limit for tetrachloroethene of 20 ppm as an eight-hour time-weighted average.

rows.source: HSE dry-cleaning solvent controls
rows.verified: HSE identifies biological monitoring as a tool that can support a workplace tetrachloroethene exposure-control strategy.

rows.source: HSE dry-cleaning solvent controls
rows.verified: HSE reports use of the Bio-VOC sampler in surveys of dry-cleaning workers exposed to tetrachloroethene.

rows.source: HSE dry-cleaning solvent controls
rows.verified: The COSHH sheet requires all listed control points, or equally effective measures, to be followed to reduce exposure adequately.

rows.source: HSE dry-cleaning solvent controls
rows.verified: Dry-cleaning solvent controls should follow the COSHH objective of preventing exposure or, where prevention is not practicable, adequately controlling it.

rows.source: HSE dry-cleaning solvent controls
rows.verified: Dry-cleaning solvent risk depends on solvent identity, machine integrity, loading and unloading, spotting, ventilation, maintenance and exposure duration.

rows.source: HSE dry-cleaning solvent controls
rows.verified: Dry-cleaning evidence is solvent-, process-, machine-, task- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level toxicity probability.
